summary: Gives the overall framework for the data plane of Deterministic Networking (DetNet), which aims to carry time-sensitive traffic with bounded latency and very low loss. It covers concepts common to any DetNet data plane and touches on related controller plane considerations.

plainLanguage.summary: Some messages, like those controlling a factory robot, must arrive on time every time. This describes the general rules for a network lane built to guarantee that.

subtitle: Framework for time-sensitive networked applications with guaranteed delivery.

tldr.problem: Real-time applications like industrial automation and financial trading need networks to guarantee low latency and minimal packet loss, but standard best-effort networks cannot provide this.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a framework with two layers: a service sub-layer for packet replication and elimination, and a forwarding sub-layer for resource reservation and explicit routing.
tldr.outcome: Enables networks to carry deterministic flows with extremely low loss and bounded latency over IP or MPLS.

today: RFC 8938 is an Informational framework from 2020. It defines the common concepts for DetNet, which is being standardized in complementary RFCs for specific data planes (RFC 8939 for IP, RFC 8926 for MPLS). DetNet is increasingly deployed in industrial networks and applications requiring deterministic behavior.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) provides the ability to carry data flows with extremely low packet loss rates and assured maximum end-to-end latency. This is needed for time-sensitive applications such as industrial control systems, power grid protection, and autonomous vehicle coordination.

This document describes the data plane framework: the packet headers and processing steps that make deterministic behavior possible. It covers the common concepts that apply to any DetNet data plane (whether based on IP or MPLS) and addresses Controller Plane (management and control) considerations.

The framework applies whether DetNet is deployed over traditional Ethernet links or over Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) from IEEE 802.1, but TSN support is not required for DetNet.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal networks try their best to deliver packets but don't promise anything. DetNet promises to deliver your packet on time, every time.

sections.title: Data Plane Architecture
sections.content:
The DetNet data plane is organized into two sub-layers. The service sub-layer adds DetNet-specific features like packet sequencing, flow replication (sending copies to increase reliability), and packet elimination (discarding duplicates). The forwarding sub-layer provides the network connectivity, resource allocation, and explicit route steering that keep latency and jitter bounded.

A DetNet node operates in stages: packets enter from applications or lower layers, pass through the service sub-layer (which may replicate packets and add sequence numbers), pass through the forwarding sub-layer (which routes and queues them), and exit to the destination. The forwarding sub-layer may use IP routing, MPLS label switching, or other technologies underneath.

The service sub-layer is optional; simple DetNet flows may only need the forwarding sub-layer for resource allocation and explicit routing.
sections.plainLanguage: A DetNet packet goes through two stages: the service layer (which might make backup copies), then the forwarding layer (which routes it carefully). Different networks might do this differently.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
DetNet flows carry two key metadata items in their packets. The Flow-ID identifies which DetNet flow a packet belongs to. A sequence number identifies the position of the packet within the flow, needed for eliminating duplicates or reordering out-of-order packets.

The service sub-layer functions include: Packet Replication Function (PRF) (making copies on different paths), Packet Elimination Function (PEF) (discarding duplicates), and Packet Ordering Function (POF) (putting packets back in order). These functions together are PREOF.

The forwarding sub-layer reserves bandwidth and assigns explicit routes based on the flow's requirements. Resource reservation ensures that each DetNet flow gets the bandwidth and buffer space it needs. Explicit routes let the controller choose the exact path a flow takes, enabling the controller to ensure latency bounds.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet packets carry an ID (which flow) and a sequence number (packet order). The network can copy packets for safety, or remove copies if they arrive twice. It also reserves bandwidth and picks the exact route to hit latency targets.

sections.title: Operational Modes: IP and MPLS
sections.content:
DetNet can operate over either IP or MPLS networks, with different encapsulation choices. For DetNet IP, packets use the 6-tuple (source and destination IP addresses, source and destination ports, protocol, and DSCP field) to identify the flow. No sequence numbers are available in native IP mode, so PREOF must be handled by adding an encapsulation like GRE or IPv6 extension headers.

For DetNet MPLS, packets are labeled with MPLS headers. The DetNet service label (S-Label) identifies the DetNet service instance, and an optional DetNet Control Word (d-CW) carries metadata like sequence numbers. This approach makes sequence numbers available for PREOF functions.

In both cases, the forwarding sub-layer operates using standard traffic engineering: explicit routes (e.g., via RSVP-TE, GMPLS, or segment routing) and resource reservations steer traffic on paths that meet latency and loss requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Over IP, DetNet identifies flows by their addresses and ports. Over MPLS, it uses labels. Each method can carry sequence numbers if needed for duplicate detection.

sections.title: Controller Plane and Configuration
sections.content:
DetNet needs a Controller Plane (which combines control and management functions) to instantiate flows, reserve resources, and compute paths. The Controller Plane must:

Set up DetNet flows in the domain by determining explicit paths, reserving link bandwidth, allocating node buffers, setting queuing disciplines, and managing bidirectional traffic. Manage label allocation (in MPLS) or flow identification (in IP). Support flow aggregation to improve scalability. Advertise node and link resources and capabilities to other controllers or routing protocols. Scale to handle the number of flows expected in the domain. Provision flow identification information at each node.

These functions can be achieved using distributed signaling (like RSVP-TE), centralized provisioning (BGP, PCEP, YANG), or hybrid approaches. All must ultimately configure the data plane identically from the perspective of packet forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone (a controller or management system) must set up each flow: choose its path, reserve bandwidth, and tell routers how to handle it. This can be done by a centralized system or by protocols that routers run themselves.

sections.title: Protection and Aggregation
sections.content:
Service protection uses multiple paths and packet replication to survive network failures. In 1:1 linear protection, two copies of each packet travel different paths, and the receiver eliminates duplicates. In 1+1 protection, the sender replicates packets, but only one path is active at a time; a standby path activates if the primary fails.

Aggregation improves scalability by treating multiple DetNet flows as a single aggregate, with shared reservation and treatment. Aggregated flows must be compatible (same or very similar latency requirements). The sum of their individual reservations must not exceed the aggregate reservation.

Applications can be Ethernet, IP, or other data types mapped on top of DetNet. Different types may use different DetNet encapsulations but can coexist in the same domain. DetNet also supports running over underlying sub-networks like IEEE 802.1 TSN, which provide link-layer timing and preemption.
sections.plainLanguage: For reliability, make backup copies on different paths. For scalability, group similar flows and treat them as one. Different applications can use DetNet, each using the encapsulation that fits it.
